name: oak
why: A small dynamic language of uncertain maturity; a possible curiosity worth a look despite thin evidence of depth.

brief.what_it_is: Oak is a small, dynamically typed, general-purpose programming language with a single-executable toolchain. The oak binary ships an interpreter and a REPL, plus a standard library, a code formatter (oak fmt), a bundler and Oak-to-JavaScript compiler (oak build), a test runner, and a documentation tool for source files. Oak source files ending in .oak are the input, and the output is either run results, a single-file bundle of Oak source, or a JavaScript bundle when built with --web. The homepage includes a sample HTTP server using http.Server and a FizzBuzz example.
brief.why_it_exists: The author built it as a sequel to their earlier toy language Ink, to correct early mistakes and be easier to read and use, and says it is for their own hobby projects. Since late 2021 it has been their main language for simple scripts, side projects, and personal knowledge tools.
brief.how_it_works: Oak is an expression-based imperative language that borrows syntax from Lua and JavaScript and leans on functional idioms, with lists, objects, atoms, and first-class functions. Its if expression works like a pattern-matching switch on deeply compared shapes of data, and the := and <- operators bind names, with <- assigning to an existing variable in an enclosing scope. Iteration is done through recursion with optimized tail calls and standard-library functions such as range, map, each, filter, and reduce, since the language has no for or while loops. The homepage also describes a with expression that places a trailing callback argument after the call, and says the bundler and compiler were built on the author's earlier Ink toolchain, September.

brief.install_notes: On macOS, brew install oak is the easy route. Without Homebrew, download the release binary to /usr/local/bin/oak and make it executable. On Linux, the same curl and chmod steps apply, and you may need sudo (sudo -s) to write into /usr/local/bin. Official release builds are for Linux and macOS on x86. Other platforms need a build from source with Go (go build -o ./oak) or a package from another repository. After installing, run oak version and add the binary to PATH if you want to drop the ./ prefix. No accounts, runtime, or configuration are mentioned beyond this.
brief.standout: The whole toolchain ships as one executable, and a program can be deployed as a single source bundle or compiled to a single JavaScript file for browser or Node use. The if expression is a structural pattern matcher over nested objects and lists, and the language has no loop keywords, relying on tail-recursive functions for iteration.
brief.status: Unknown from the homepage alone. The site itself says Oak is still under construction and that official documentation will come when the language is more finished. It says the core language and basic standard libraries are complete but still too unstable to call ready, and that the author has been building it since early July 2021. The REPL example timestamp is 2022-01-27 and the version shown is v0.2, which suggests the page was last written around early 2022. I did not check the GitHub repository for release or commit dates.
brief.caveats: The homepage says Oak is still under construction, with official docs not yet written and a very bare site. The author calls the core unstable. Official release builds exist only for Linux and macOS on x86. Oak is strongly typed with no implicit casting, but the page calls it dynamically typed, which reads as a mismatch in terms. You cannot remove values from the middle of a list, and object key order is not preserved. There are no loops, only recursion. The planned oak compile command that would package the interpreter into a binary does not exist yet. The page does not state a license.
quotes: Oak is still under construction! Official documentation for Oak will be available when the language is more finished.
Oak is a sequel to Ink that tries to correct many of these early mistakes, while being easier to read and use.
Oak is intentionally not "Ink 2.0" — it's not a simple upgrade or bug fix, but a different language with many well-considered updates in the details.
